lesson.title: Which Way Does It Go? Predicting Spontaneity with Entropy
lesson.summary: The second law says a process is spontaneous only if it increases the total entropy of the universe, and splitting that total into a system term and a surroundings term shows why the same process can be spontaneous at one temperature and not at another.
lesson.body:
Entropy, as introduced in the previous chapter, is a state function that increases as energy and matter become more spread out. To decide whether a process actually happens on its own, spontaneously, the second law of thermodynamics requires looking at the entropy change of the entire universe, which is conveniently split into two pieces: the system, the specific substance or reaction being studied, and the surroundings, everything else that can exchange heat with it. Formally, delta S(universe) = delta S(system) + delta S(surroundings), and a process is spontaneous if and only if delta S(universe) is positive.

The system's entropy change, delta S(system), can often be estimated from structural reasoning (more gas moles, more freedom of motion, higher temperature all tend to increase it) or calculated from tabulated data, as the next chapter, standard entropy, will show. The surroundings' entropy change is calculated differently: at constant temperature and pressure, heat leaving or entering the system enters or leaves the surroundings, and delta S(surroundings) = -delta H(system) / T. The negative sign matters: when the system releases heat (delta H(system) is negative, an exothermic process), that heat flows into the surroundings and increases the surroundings' entropy, so delta S(surroundings) comes out positive. This term is exactly the delta H over T relationship from the previous chapter, just applied to the surroundings instead of to a phase transition of the system itself.

Here is why temperature can flip spontaneity, using the water-freezing numbers built in the previous chapter. Freezing is the reverse of melting, so its enthalpy and entropy changes are the melting values with the sign flipped: delta H(sys, freezing) = -6.01 kJ/mol = -6010 J/mol, and delta S(sys, freezing) = -22.0 J/(mol K), since a liquid becoming a solid loses freedom of arrangement. First, consider freezing at -10 degrees Celsius, 263 K, a temperature below water's normal freezing point. delta S(surroundings) = -delta H(sys) / T = -(-6010 J/mol) / 263 K = 6010 / 263 = about +22.85 J/(mol K). Adding the system and surroundings terms: delta S(universe) = -22.0 + 22.85 = about +0.85 J/(mol K). Since this is positive, freezing is spontaneous at -10 C, which matches everyday experience: water left in a freezer does turn to ice on its own.

Now repeat the calculation at +10 degrees Celsius, 283 K, above the normal freezing point. delta S(surroundings) = 6010 / 283 = about +21.24 J/(mol K). This time delta S(universe) = -22.0 + 21.24 = about -0.76 J/(mol K), which is negative, meaning freezing is not spontaneous at 10 C. That also matches everyday experience: liquid water sitting at 10 C does not spontaneously freeze. Nothing about the system's own entropy change or enthalpy change actually changed between these two calculations; only the surroundings term shifted, because the same amount of released heat has a proportionally larger entropic effect on colder surroundings than on warmer ones. This is the mechanical reason temperature appears in every discussion of spontaneity: it is not that molecules behave differently at different temperatures, it is that the 1/T factor in the surroundings' entropy term changes how much that heat transfer is worth, entropically, at different temperatures.
